qc.label_under_test: A second, mirrored labelling clause that casts the speaker or the listener: after one clause casts someone as something (sees him as a hero, calls her a liar), a following clause casts me, us or you (and she sees me as a nuisance, they treat us as outsiders, and he calls you a snob); it fires on the 'as' or 'a' right after 'me'/'us'/'you'. 'You' fires when you did the first labelling (you treat them as family, and they treat you as staff); after 'I see him as...', a second clause casting you stays weak. The same second clause aimed at him, her or them is weak, as is a one-way label of me or you with no earlier labelling clause, or me labelled in the first clause and answering back. Strongest when a sentence of setting comes first.

neighbours.label: A second, mirrored labelling clause that turns a label around: after one clause casts someone as something (treats, sees, calls or considers a person as or as a ...), a following clause casts the speaker or listener (me, us, you), or casts back the very person who did the first labelling (by name or as him/her); it fires on the 'as' or 'a' right after that object. The second clause can follow 'and', 'while' or a new sentence. It stays weak when the second clause casts a newcomer not in the first clause, a group or a thing, and for a single labelling clause with no earlier one. Strongest when a sentence of setting comes first.
fire: The office was quiet that Monday. Laura treats her boss as a mentor, while he sees her as a threat.
We met at the harbor last summer. Tom calls me a genius, and I call him a liar.
The village had one school and one bakery. The teacher considered Maria a troublemaker, and Maria considered the teacher a bully.
It rained all through the tournament. You see him as a hero, while he sees you as a rival.
Our team moved into the new building in spring. The manager treats Ahmed as an intern. Ahmed treats him as a fool.
The party was loud and crowded. She regards him as a friend, and he regards her as a stranger.
Snow covered the campus that winter. Professor Lin sees Daniel as a slacker, while Daniel sees Lin as a tyrant.
The kitchen smelled of bread. Grandma treats my brother as a baby, and he treats us as servants.
quiet: The office was quiet that Monday. Laura treats her boss as a mentor, and she brings him coffee every morning.
We met at the harbor last summer. Tom calls me a genius at parties.
The village had one school and one bakery. The teacher considered Maria a troublemaker, and the baker considered the weather a nuisance.
It rained all through the tournament. You see him as a hero, while the fans see the trophy as a curse.
Our team moved into the new building in spring. The manager treats Ahmed as an intern, and he answers every email quickly.
The party was loud and crowded. She regards him as a friend and laughs at his jokes.
Snow covered the campus that winter. Professor Lin sees Daniel as a slacker, while a visiting dean sees the department as a mess.
The kitchen smelled of bread. Grandma treats my brother as a baby, and she bakes him cookies daily.
